sojourn

SOH-jurn · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Sojourn is a temporary stay in a place.

The explorer's journal describes a lengthy sojourn among a remote island community, where he learned their language and customs before continuing his voyage.

Example

After the earthquake, the family's brief sojourn with relatives in another city stretched into nearly six months while their home was rebuilt.

A sojourn is a temporary stay somewhere, not a permanent move -- here, the family always intended to return home once repairs were finished.

Your Turn

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

stay: A stay is any period spent in a place — one night in a hotel, a week in the hospital, a whole summer at the lake — and the word promises nothing about what kind. A sojourn is always temporary by intention: you sojourn somewhere planning to move on or return home.

stopover: A stopover is a brief pause in the middle of a journey — a night, an afternoon — made only on the way to somewhere else. A sojourn is a real temporary stay: you unpack, settle in for days or months, and live there for a while before moving on.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

permanence: the state of lasting or staying forever, the opposite of a temporary stay

departure: the act of leaving, the opposite of settling in for a stay

Where it sits · how long and settled the stay is — visit → sojourn → residency

visit vs. sojourn: A visit is a very brief, often informal call on a place, much shorter than an extended sojourn.

residency vs. sojourn: A residency is an extended, often formal period of living somewhere, longer and more settled than a typical sojourn.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — so- / sub-

prefix — so- / sub-: under, during (Latin)

root — -journ-

root — -journ-: day (Latin diurnus, via Old French journee)

Put it together

Put it together: Sojourn comes from Old French sojourner, built on Latin sub- ('during') plus diurnus ('daily, of a day'). It originally meant simply 'to stay for a while, day by day.' The same day- root, journee, gives us the everyday word journal -- originally a daily record.

Use the root in a new word: journal

Use the root in a new word: journal: She kept a detailed journal during her travels, writing a new entry every single day.
